## `radix_sort::insert_sort`

[source](radix_sort.goose#L46-L48)

```goose
checkfree fn insert_sort<V>(slice: V[:])
```

Sort slice in place with insertion sort, comparing its values directly.
This sort is stable and works well for small or nearly sorted inputs.

```goose
let values = [4, 1, 3, 1];
radix_sort::insert_sort(values);
assert(values == [1, 1, 3, 4]);
```

<a id="api-2"></a>

## `radix_sort::insert_sort`

[source](radix_sort.goose#L66-L78)

```goose
checkfree fn insert_sort<V, Key: fn(V) -> T>(slice: V[:])
```

Sort slice in place with insertion sort, comparing values through Key.
Key must be callable from a `checkfree` function. Equal-key values retain
their original order.

Define key functions at top level so they can be `checkfree`:

```goose ignore
checkfree fn low_byte(value: u16) -> u16 { value & 0xFF }
```

```goose
let values: u16[] = [0x102, 0x001, 0x100];
radix_sort::insert_sort(values, low_byte);
let expected: u16[] = [0x100, 0x001, 0x102];
assert(values == expected);
```

<a id="api-3"></a>

## `radix_sort::radix_sort`

[source](radix_sort.goose#L92-L94)

```goose
fn radix_sort<V>(slice: V[:])
```

Sort signed or unsigned integers in place with an MSD radix sort.

The sort is not stable. Inputs of at most 64 elements use insertion sort;
larger inputs process the most-significant byte first and recursively refine
each bucket. Empty slices are accepted.

```goose
let values: u16[] = [500, 1, 256, 0, 255];
radix_sort::radix_sort(values);
let expected: u16[] = [0, 1, 255, 256, 500];
assert(values == expected);
```

<a id="api-4"></a>

## `radix_sort::radix_sort`

[source](radix_sort.goose#L116-L123)

```goose
fn radix_sort<V, Key: fn(V) -> T>(slice: V[:])
```

Sort values in place by the integer returned by Key.

Key must return an `i8`–`i64` or `u8`–`u64` and must be callable from a
`checkfree` function. Signed keys are normalized so negative values sort
before nonnegative values. The sort is not stable, so values with equal keys
may be reordered. The complete value is moved during partitioning; payload
data remains attached to its key.

Define key functions at top level so they can be `checkfree`:

```goose ignore
checkfree fn low_byte(value: u16) -> u16 { value & 0xFF }
```

```goose
let values: u16[] = [0x102, 0x001, 0x100];
radix_sort::radix_sort(values, low_byte);
let expected: u16[] = [0x100, 0x001, 0x102];
assert(values == expected);
```

## `iitree::Interval`

[source](iitree.goose#L31-L36)

```goose
struct Interval<V> {
    start: i32,
    max:   i32,
    stop:  i32,
    value: V,
}
```

A half-open interval `start..stop` on one contig, carrying a value.

max belongs to the tree: until `index` it is the number of the interval's
contig, and afterwards the largest stop in the interval's subtree. start
and max are adjacent so that they load as one sort key.

```goose
let tree = iitree::IITree<u8> { .. };
tree.add("chr1", 10, 20, 'a');
tree.index();
tree.overlap("chr1", 15, 16) { interval =>
    assert(interval.start == 10 && interval.stop == 20 && interval.value == 'a');
};
```

## `iitree::Contig`

[source](iitree.goose#L49-L53)

```goose
struct Contig {
    root_k: i32,
    offset: i64,
    count:  i64,
}
```

One contig's part of the tree: `intervals[offset..offset + count]`, a tree
of height root_k. root_k is -1 for a contig without intervals.

```goose
let tree = iitree::IITree<i32> { .. };
tree.add("chr1", 10, 20, 0);
tree.add("chr2", 5, 8, 1);
tree.add("chr2", 6, 9, 2);
tree.index();
assert(tree.contigs[1].offset == 1 && tree.contigs[1].count == 2);
```

## `iitree::IITree`

[source](iitree.goose#L71-L76)

```goose
root struct IITree<V> {
    intervals:  Interval<V>[>..]             = [],
    contigs:    Contig[>..]                  = [],
    names:      u8[varint][>..]              = [],
    contig_ids: dictionary<const u8[:], i32> = dictionary<const u8[:], i32> {},
}
```

Intervals with values of type V, grouped by contig. Construct one with
`IITree<V> { .. }`, `add` every interval, call `index` once, and then query
with `overlap`.

Contigs are numbered in the order `add` first sees their names; contig_ids
maps a name, kept in names, to that number.

```goose
let tree = iitree::IITree<i32> { .. };
tree.add("chr1", 10, 20, 0);
tree.add("chr1", 30, 40, 1);
tree.index();
var hits = 0;
tree.overlap("chr1", 19, 31) { interval => hits += 1; };
assert(hits == 2);
```

## `iitree::add`

[source](iitree.goose#L105-L109)

```goose
fn add<V>(tree: IITree<V>&, contig: const u8[:], start: i32, stop: i32, value: V)
```

Add the interval `start..stop` of contig, with its value, to a tree that is
not yet indexed. An interval whose start is after its stop is ignored.

```goose
let tree = iitree::IITree<f64> { .. };
tree.add("chr1", 10, 20, 0.5);
tree.add("chr1", 20, 10, 1.5); // Ignored.
assert(tree.intervals.len == 1 && tree.intervals[0].value == 0.5);
```

## `iitree::index`

[source](iitree.goose#L126-L149)

```goose
fn index<V>(tree: IITree<V>&)
```

Sort the intervals by contig and start, then build each contig's tree.
Call it once, after the last `add` and before the first `overlap`.

```goose
let tree = iitree::IITree<i32> { .. };
tree.add("chr1", 30, 40, 1);
tree.add("chr1", 10, 20, 0);
tree.index();
assert(tree.intervals[0].value == 0 && tree.intervals[1].value == 1);
```

<a id="api-11"></a>

## `iitree::overlap`

[source](iitree.goose#L211-L249)

```goose
fn overlap<V, F: fn(Interval<V>&)>(tree: IITree<V>&, contig: const u8[:], start: i32, stop: i32)
```

Call F with every interval of contig that overlaps `start..stop`, in order
of interval start. An unknown contig has no overlaps. The tree must be
indexed.

```goose
let tree = iitree::IITree<i32> { .. };
tree.add("chr1", 10, 20, 0);
tree.add("chr1", 15, 25, 1);
tree.add("chr1", 30, 40, 2);
tree.add("chr2", 10, 20, 3);
tree.index();
var values: i32[>..] = [];
tree.overlap("chr1", 19, 30) { interval => values.push(interval.value); };
let expected: i32[] = [0, 1]; // Half-open: 30..40 only touches the query.
assert(values == expected);
```

## `lapper::overlap`

[source](lapper.goose#L51-L53)

```goose
inline fn overlap<T, V>(a: Interval<T, V>&, b: Interval<T, V>&) -> bool
```

Whether a and b share a position. Intervals that only touch do not overlap.

```goose
let a = lapper::Interval<i32, u8> { 10, 20, 'a' };
let b = lapper::Interval<i32, u8> { 19, 30, 'b' };
let c = lapper::Interval<i32, u8> { 20, 30, 'c' };
assert(lapper::overlap(a, b));
assert(!lapper::overlap(a, c));
```

```goose
inline fn overlap<T, V>(a: Interval<T, V>&, b_start: T, b_stop: T) -> bool
```

```goose
let a = lapper::Interval<i32, u8> { 10, 20, 'a' };
assert(lapper::overlap(a, 19, 30));
assert(!lapper::overlap(a, 0, 10));
```

## `lapper::Lapper`

[source](lapper.goose#L88-L103)

```goose
struct Lapper<T, V> {
    // The intervals by start, then stop. Block b is intervals[b * BLOCK..(b + 1) * BLOCK].
    intervals:   Interval<T, V>[:],
    // The start and stop of every interval, padded to whole blocks.
    starts:      T[:],
    stops:       T[:],
    // Each block's first start, its smallest stop, and the largest stop of
    // the blocks up to and including it.
    block_start: T[:],
    block_min:   T[:],
    prefix_max:  T[:],
    // A binary tree of the blocks' largest stops with leaves leaves: node i
    // has the children 2 * i and 2 * i + 1, and block b is node leaves + b.
    tree:        T[:],
    leaves:      i64,
}
```

One sequence's intervals, sorted and indexed for `find`. Make one with
`new_lapper`. Its fields are slices of the two arrays passed to
`new_lapper`, so a Lapper is a plain value: keep one per chromosome in an
array, and keep both arrays alive and their intervals unchanged while it
is in use. Everything but intervals is the index.

```goose
let chr1: lapper::Interval<i32, u8>[>..] = [
    lapper::Interval<i32, u8> { 0, 10, 'a' },
    lapper::Interval<i32, u8> { 5, 15, 'b' },
];
let chr2: lapper::Interval<i32, u8>[>..] = [lapper::Interval<i32, u8> { 100, 110, 'c' }];
var index: i32[>..] = [];
var lappers: lapper::Lapper<i32, u8>[>..] = [];
lappers.push(lapper::new_lapper(chr1, index));
lappers.push(lapper::new_lapper(chr2, index));

var found: u8[>..] = [];
lappers[0].find(7, 9) { interval => found.push(interval.val); };
lappers[1].find(105, 106) { interval => found.push(interval.val); };
assert(found == "abc");
```

<a id="api-16"></a>

## `lapper::new_lapper`

[source](lapper.goose#L138-L192)

```goose
fn new_lapper<T, V>(intervals: Interval<T, V>[:], index: T[>..]&) -> Lapper<T, V>
```

Sort intervals in place by start, then stop, and index them. The index is
appended to index, 2 T per interval plus 5 T per block of 32; the result
holds slices of both arguments. One index array can serve any number of
Lappers. Intervals that are already in order are not sorted again.

```goose
let intervals: lapper::Interval<i32, u8>[>..] = [
    lapper::Interval<i32, u8> { 20, 30, 'c' },
    lapper::Interval<i32, u8> { 0, 10, 'b' },
    lapper::Interval<i32, u8> { 0, 5, 'a' },
];
var index: i32[>..] = [];
let sorted = lapper::new_lapper(intervals, index);
assert(sorted.intervals.len == 3 && index.len > 0);
assert(intervals[0].val == 'a' && intervals[1].val == 'b' && intervals[2].val == 'c');
```

## `lapper::find`

[source](lapper.goose#L287-L314)

```goose
fn find<T, V, F: fn(Interval<T, V>&)>(lapper: Lapper<T, V>&, start: T, stop: T)
```

Call F with every interval that overlaps `start..stop`, ordered by start,
then stop.

```goose
let intervals: lapper::Interval<i32, u8>[>..] = [
    lapper::Interval<i32, u8> { 0, 10, 'a' },
    lapper::Interval<i32, u8> { 8, 12, 'b' },
    lapper::Interval<i32, u8> { 20, 30, 'c' },
    lapper::Interval<i32, u8> { 30, 40, 'd' },
];
var index: i32[>..] = [];
let exons = lapper::new_lapper(intervals, index);

var found: u8[>..] = [];
exons.find(9, 25) { interval => found.push(interval.val); };
assert(found == "abc");

found.clear();
exons.find(12, 20) { interval => found.push(interval.val); };
assert(found.len == 0);
```

## `fastx::Stream`

[source](fastx.goose#L31-L38)

```goose
struct Stream {
    file:   io::FileHandle,
    begin:  i64  = 0,
    end:    i64  = 0,
    is_eof: bool = false,
    failed: bool = false,
    buffer: u8[BUFFER_SIZE],
}
```

A file read through a buffer whose unread bytes are `buffer[begin..end]`;
kseq.h's `kstream_t`. Construct one with `Stream { file: file, .. }`. It
does not close the file.

```goose
let file, opened = io::open_read("tests/example.fq");
assert(opened);
let reader = fastx::Reader { stream: fastx::Stream { file: file, .. } };
defer io::close(reader.stream.file);
assert(reader.read() == fastx::Status.Record);
assert(!reader.stream.failed);
```

<a id="api-19"></a>

## `fastx::Status`

[source](fastx.goose#L118-L126)

```goose
enum Status {
    Record,
    // The input has no more records.
    End,
    // A FASTQ record's quality is missing or not as long as its sequence.
    Truncated,
    // The file could not be read.
    Failed,
}
```

What `read` found.

```goose
let file, opened = io::open_read("tests/example.fq");
assert(opened);
let reader = fastx::Reader { stream: fastx::Stream { file: file, .. } };
defer io::close(reader.stream.file);
var records = 0;
var status = reader.read();
while status == fastx::Status.Record {
    records += 1;
    status = reader.read();
}
assert(records == 2 && status == fastx::Status.End);
```

## `fastx::Reader`

[source](fastx.goose#L142-L151)

```goose
root struct Reader {
    name:    u8[>..] = [],
    comment: u8[>..] = [],
    seq:     u8[>..] = [],
    qual:    u8[>..] = [],
    // The `>` or `@` of the next record when reading a sequence consumed it,
    // otherwise 0.
    last_char: i32 = 0,
    stream:    Stream,
}
```

The most recently read record and the stream it came from; kseq.h's
`kseq_t`. name is the header up to its first whitespace and comment the
rest of the header line; qual is empty for a FASTA record. `read` replaces
all four.

```goose
let file, opened = io::open_read("tests/example.fq");
assert(opened);
let reader = fastx::Reader { stream: fastx::Stream { file: file, .. } };
defer io::close(reader.stream.file);
assert(reader.read() == fastx::Status.Record);
assert(reader.name == "read1" && reader.comment == "first read");
assert(reader.seq == "ACGTACGT" && reader.qual == "IIIIHHHH");
```

<a id="api-21"></a>

## `fastx::read`

[source](fastx.goose#L166-L204)

```goose
fn read(reader: Reader&) -> Status
```

Read the next record into reader, as `kseq_read` does, and return what was
found. After `Truncated` the fields hold what the record had; after `End`
or `Failed` they are not meaningful.

```goose
let file, opened = io::open_read("tests/example.fq");
assert(opened);
let reader = fastx::Reader { stream: fastx::Stream { file: file, .. } };
defer io::close(reader.stream.file);
var bases = 0;
while reader.read() == fastx::Status.Record { bases += reader.seq.len; }
assert(bases == 12);
```
